GLEUHR
Front Desk Function  •  The Front Desk Manager
Aesthetic Medicine
FDM Playbook
Version 1.0   |   The Conductor of the Floor, the Bridge Between Operations and Care
The doctor holds the consultation.
The counsellor holds the plan.
The therapist holds the cabin.
You hold the whole floor — the patients, the team, the schedule, the standard, the small problems that would become big ones if you did not catch them in the corridor.

This playbook is about how you hold the floor without anyone feeling held.


The FDM's Inner Stance
Read this before the morning huddle. It takes one minute. It is the difference between a floor that runs and a floor that runs you.
What the floor is actually carrying
The reception team is bracing for the first calls of the day. The therapists are checking trolleys. The doctor is reviewing the day's list. The housekeeping team is finishing the last hour of pre-opening reset. Every one of them is operating in their own quiet pressure — the receptionist worried about the patient who said she might cancel, the therapist worried about the procedure she has not done in two weeks, the doctor worried about being on time for an early consult.
Your job is to walk into all of that and absorb it. Not by being everywhere — you cannot — but by being the steady person they all reach toward when something tightens. The floor's heart rate is yours. When you are calm, they are calm. When you are stressed, the whole branch tastes it within an hour.
The supervisor trap
FDMs are sometimes promoted from the desk because they were good at the desk. The instinct is to keep doing the desk work, just with a slightly bigger badge — answering phones, processing payments, escalating to the BM. That is not the role. The role is to make the desk run so well that you almost never have to touch it. Your work is in the corridors, in the cabin handovers, in the patient who is about to cancel, in the team member who is having a bad morning.
INNER STANCE  The desk does not need your hands. It needs your eyes and your standard. If you are answering phones for an hour because reception is slammed, you are not failing — but you are also not in the role. Either staff the desk better, or build a system that handles the spike. Doing the work yourself feels productive in the moment and creates a fragile clinic over time.
Your three jobs on this floor
1.  Run the day — the morning huddle, the patient flow, the handovers between team members, the end-of-day debrief. Smoothly, every day, without drama.
2.  Hold the standard — reception warmth, cabin reset quality, washroom freshness, complaint handling. You audit without making people feel watched. They should know you check, and they should not feel chased.
3.  Catch what would fall — the patient who is wavering on her package, the team member who is upset, the doctor running thirty minutes late, the complaint surfacing in the corridor. Catch it before it lands.
The FDM you should be
Picture the most respected stage manager you have ever seen — the one who runs the show from the wings, who knows where every actor is at every moment, who fixes problems before the audience sees them, who never once steals a scene. That is the energy. Calm. Vigilant. Unflappable. Almost invisible to the patient — highly visible, in a steadying way, to the team.
0.  Before the Day Starts  —  The Forty-Five Minutes Before First Patient
Your day starts before the team's day starts. The morning you give the floor begins with what you set up in this window.
Walk the clinic in full — reception, waiting area, washroom, every cabin, doctor's room, counsellor's room. Look at it as a patient walking in for the first time. What does the eye go to? What looks tired? Fix it now, or call housekeeping to.
Read the day's appointment list. Mark VIPs, returning complaint patients, doctor-counsellor handovers that need attention, anyone who tried to cancel and was retained, any patient flagged in the last visit notes.
Check yesterday's debrief notes. Anything unresolved — a patient who needs a callback, a billing dispute, a complaint pending response. Get those on today's first hour, not floating into the afternoon.
Confirm staffing — who is in, who is late, who is on leave, who is covering. If there is a gap, solve it before 9 am, not at 11 when the floor is hot.
Take a breath. Whatever is happening in your personal life right now stays on this side of the floor door.
AVOID  Do not enter the floor still on a phone call. Do not enter visibly stressed. Do not enter in a hurry. The team reads your morning in the first ninety seconds of seeing you. If you walk in tight, every conversation today is going to be slightly tight.
1.  The Morning Huddle  —  Ten Minutes That Set the Day
The moment
Eight forty-five. The team is gathered. Receptionist, counsellor, therapists, housekeeping, doctor if she joins. This is the only block of the day when you have all of them at once, calm, before the patients arrive. Use it deliberately.
The structure  —  every morning, same shape
Yesterday in one sentence. "Yesterday we did 22 walk-ins, 14 conversions, one complaint resolved by Jaspreet ma'am. Good day overall."
Today's patient highlights. Two or three names that matter — a VIP, a returning complaint follow-up, a tricky case. "Mrs Khanna is in at 11 — returning for her second microneedling, very pleased last time, please greet her warmly. Mrs Sharma at 3:30 — her first session was uncomfortable, doctor will spend extra time with her, please do not rush her at reception."
One thing we are working on this week. A focused improvement — cabin reset times, washroom audit completion, post-treatment follow-up calls. One thing. Not five.
Anything from the team. Open the floor for thirty seconds. If anyone has an issue, this is the safest moment of the day to raise it.
Close warmly. "Have a good day, team. Let's take care of each other and the patients."
FIRST AFFIRMATION  ·  THE MORNING CLOSE
“Have a good day, team. Let's take care of each other and the patients.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The morning huddle is not an information transfer. It is the team's first emotional reading of the day. If you stand straight, speak warmly, and close with that one line, the team starts the day forty percent steadier. If you read the list flatly, fiddle with your phone, and leave without warmth — you have just delivered a sub-standard day to every patient walking in over the next eight hours.
AVOID  Do not turn the huddle into a critique. Public corrections — ‘Jaspreet, you missed the washroom check yesterday’ — humiliate the person and bruise the whole team. Save individual corrections for one-to-one moments. The huddle is for direction and warmth, not discipline.
2.  The Floor Walk  —  Auditing Without Making Anyone Feel Watched
Two floor walks a day, minimum. One mid-morning when the floor is busy. One late afternoon when the standard tends to slip from fatigue. Each walk takes ten minutes.
What you are looking at
Reception — desk clean, receptionist looking up at patients, phone within reach not in use, water available, dustbin not full.
Waiting area — cushions plumped, magazines current, no patient sitting unattended for more than ten minutes without acknowledgement.
Washroom — hourly check signed, tissue stocked, floor dry, smell fresh, dustbin under one-third.
Corridors — no clutter, no used-linen baskets in patient sight, no staff conversations within earshot of waiting patients.
Cabins (between patients only) — reset complete, linen fresh, trolley aligned, fragrance set.
Pantry — water stocked, glasses clean, surfaces wiped.
Team energy — who looks tense, who is moving slower than usual, who looks like they need a moment.
How you walk
Slowly. Warmly. Smile at every staff member you pass. Greet each one by name. Pause at the desk briefly to ask the receptionist how the morning is going. Stop by the cabin between patients and ask the therapist if her last patient was okay. The walk should feel like a senior person checking on her people, not a supervisor inspecting them.
INNER STANCE  The fastest way to lose your team's trust is to walk the floor with a checklist visible and a frown. The fastest way to keep it is to walk the floor without a checklist visible — and to notice ten things in your head and remember every one of them in the one-to-one conversations later. The team should feel cared about. The standard should feel held. Both can be true at once if you walk well.
3.  The Correction Conversation  —  Said Quietly, Said Once
You will see things on the floor that need fixing. A cabin reset that was incomplete. A reception greeting that lacked warmth. A washroom check missed. The wrong move is to correct in the corridor in front of others. The right move is to wait, find a private moment within the next hour, and have a short, kind, specific conversation.
What you say
“Hi [Name], can I borrow you for two minutes? Just one thing I want to mention from this morning. When I walked the cabin after Mrs Sharma left, the trolley wasn't fully aligned and there was a tissue on the floor. Small thing, but it would have been the first thing the next patient saw. Just stay sharp on the two-second test before you leave the cabin. Everything else this morning has been good. Thanks.”
The structure of every correction
Specific moment. Not ‘you have been slipping’ — say what, when, where.
Why it matters. Not as a rule, but as an impact. ‘The next patient would have seen it.’
The fix. One sentence. Clear.
Acknowledge what is going well. Genuine, not pasted on.
Move on. Do not bring it up again unless it repeats.
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The team member who is corrected privately, specifically, and warmly, comes out of that conversation more loyal than before. The team member who is corrected publicly, vaguely, or harshly, comes out of it secretly looking for another job. Same correction, same standard — completely different downstream consequences. The conversation is the lever; the standard is the constant.
4.  Patient Flow  —  Handling the Queue Without Making It Visible
The floor is going to get busy. Three patients in the waiting area, doctor running late, two cabins occupied, the counsellor finishing with someone. This is the moment the FDM exists for.
What you do
Stand near the waiting area without standing in it. Make eye contact with each waiting patient. The patient who has been acknowledged by the manager waits twice as patiently as the one who has not.
Speak to the receptionist quietly — ‘give Mrs Sharma a status update.’ Do not direct the receptionist loudly. Patients read every word.
If a wait is going to exceed twenty minutes, walk to the patient yourself. ‘[Name]ji, the doctor is wrapping up — she will be with you in about fifteen more minutes. Thank you so much for your patience. Can I get you a fresh glass of water?’
If the wait is going to exceed forty minutes, offer to reschedule with a small concession. ‘We have completely fallen behind today — I am so sorry. Would you like to reschedule for tomorrow morning, or wait? If you choose to reschedule, I would like to send you home with [a small considered gesture].’
What you say to the waiting patient who has not yet complained
“[Name]ji, I am so sorry about the wait — we had an unexpected delay with the previous consultation. The doctor is finishing now and will be with you in just a few minutes. Thank you for your patience — it really matters to us.”
SECOND AFFIRMATION  ·  THE PATIENT IN WAIT
“Thank you for your patience — it really matters to us.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The patient who is told why she is waiting, by someone in authority, will wait twice as long without complaint. The patient who has been sitting unacknowledged for twenty-five minutes is one minute away from a public scene. The FDM who walks to the waiting patient before the patient walks to the FDM has just prevented the entire afternoon from going sideways.
5.  The Hidden Complaint  —  What No One Tells You
Most patient complaints are not made at the desk. They are made in the parking lot, on the phone to a friend, in a Google review three weeks later. The FDM's job is to catch the unspoken complaint before it becomes a posted one. You will only catch it if you go looking.
The signals
A patient who walks out of a cabin quieter than she walked in.
A patient who pays without saying goodbye warmly.
A patient who declines to book the next appointment when she had been planning to.
A patient whose companion looks unhappy.
A returning patient whose pattern of warmth has dropped a notch from last visit.
What you do
Catch her at the desk or the door, gently.
“[Name]ji, before you go — I just wanted to check in. Was everything okay today? Sometimes things are small enough that we do not catch them ourselves — I would much rather hear it now than miss it.”
She may say ‘no, it was fine’ — in which case you have at least signalled that we care. She may, with the door open, say the small thing she was carrying. Either way, you have done the work.
INNER STANCE  Every patient who walks out unhappy without telling us is a future negative review and a permanent loss of a customer who would have responded to a single warm question. The hidden complaint is the highest-leverage signal you can train yourself to read. The FDM who walks to the patient with that one question is the FDM who saves the branch four reviews a month.
6.  “I Want to Speak to the Manager”  —  The Live Complaint
A patient is at the desk, visibly upset. The receptionist has called you. The waiting area can hear. This is one of the moments your job exists for.
What you do  —  in this exact order
Walk over calmly. Not slowly enough to seem indifferent, not quickly enough to seem panicked. Steady.
Introduce yourself by name and role. ‘[Name]ji, I am [your name], the manager here.’ Hearing your role lowers her need to escalate further.
Move her. The complaint must not be witnessed by other patients. ‘Please come with me to my room, we can talk properly.’ If she resists moving, sit beside her where she is.
Listen. Fully. Do not interrupt. Do not defend. Do not explain. Sixty to ninety seconds of pure listening.
Acknowledge specifically. Not ‘I understand’ — say what you understand. ‘What I am hearing is that you waited forty-five minutes today, the doctor did not address the concern you raised about your previous session, and the counsellor's tone in the room felt rushed. Have I got that right?’
Apologise without litigating. ‘That should not have happened. I am sorry. Let me make this right.’
Resolve, or commit clearly to resolving. If it is operational, fix it now — free session, refund of the wait, a fresh consultation with the doctor today. If it is clinical, get the doctor or BM involved before the patient leaves.
Document. Same hour, into the file and the complaint log. The patient's name, what she said, what was promised, who will follow up, and when.
Personally follow up within 48 hours. A call from you, asking how she is feeling now. This is the call that turns a near-loss into a five-year client.
What you say
“I am so sorry this has happened, [Name]ji. You are absolutely right to bring this to me. Please come with me — let me hear the full story properly, and let me find a way to make this right.”
THE PSYCHOLOGY  Almost no patient who escalates is asking primarily for compensation. She is asking to be heard, believed, and treated as if her complaint matters. The FDM who delivers those three things, in that order, defuses ninety per cent of complaints before any compensation is even discussed. The FDM who jumps to ‘we can offer you a free session’ too early signals that the goal is to make the complaint go away, not to address it — and the patient feels that, and escalates further.
AVOID  Do not say ‘that has never happened before.’ Do not say ‘our policy is’ in the first three minutes. Do not say ‘the doctor / therapist / counsellor would not have done that.’ Do not promise a refund you cannot deliver without checking with the BM. Do not let the conversation be witnessed in the open waiting area.
7.  The Team Member Having a Bad Day
You will see it. A therapist who is uncharacteristically curt with a patient. A receptionist whose smile is not reaching her eyes. A counsellor who is moving through the day on autopilot. Something is off. Address it — gently, today.
What you do
Wait until you can pull them aside privately, between patients. Not in the corridor, not in earshot of the team.
Ask, do not assume. ‘Hi [Name], can I borrow you for two minutes? You have seemed a little down today — is everything okay?’
Listen if she shares. Do not problem-solve unless she asks. The asking itself is most of the work.
Adjust the day if you can. ‘Take the next consult instead of the next cabin — the cabin can be covered.’ ‘Take fifteen minutes upstairs, no rush.’
If it is something larger — family issue, health, mental health — escalate quietly to the BM and offer real support.
INNER STANCE  The team member who feels noticed on her hard day will work twice as hard for you for the next two years. The team member whose hard day was pretended-not-to-see quietly leaves — sometimes the job, sometimes just the loyalty. Five minutes of warm attention is the cheapest retention investment a manager can ever make.
8.  The Doctor Running Late  —  Managing Without Panic
The doctor's morning has slipped. The 10 am consultation ran to 10:50. The 10:30 patient is waiting in the lobby. The 11 am has just arrived. The 11:30 will be here in twenty minutes. The afternoon list is going to compress, and someone is going to feel it.
What you do
Inform every waiting patient personally before they ask. ‘I am so sorry — we are running about twenty-five minutes behind today. Let me get you settled with water; the doctor will be with you as soon as possible.’
Decide which patients absolutely must be seen today, and which could be offered a courteous reschedule with a small concession. Offer the reschedule before the patient has to ask.
Brief the doctor, between patients, in one sentence. ‘We are running 25 behind, three patients waiting, the 11:30 is okay to push by twenty minutes, the 12 is a returning patient who has come from far — please prioritise her.’
Brief the counsellor. ‘Doctor handovers will start ten minutes behind today. Please slow your own conversations slightly so we don't compound it.’
Brief the therapists. ‘Your first slots may shift by 15-20 minutes — just so you have a heads-up.’
Do not snap at the doctor. The doctor running late knows she is running late. Adding pressure makes the consultations worse, which makes the day worse. Hold the floor for her so she can hold the patient.
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The doctor whose floor manager protects her on a late morning will protect the brand on every difficult patient she ever sees. The doctor whose floor manager visibly stresses about her running late will start cutting consultations short — which is the worst outcome for every patient and the brand. Your steadiness in this moment is what allows clinical excellence to continue under operational pressure.
9.  Escalation to the BM  —  When, How, and How Often
You report to the Branch Manager. She runs the branch; you run the floor. The line between what you handle and what she handles is sometimes blurry, especially when something has just happened. A simple rule:
Escalate immediately if
Any patient mentions a clinical reaction, social media, a review, or legal action.
Any patient requests a refund.
Any team member alleges harassment, discrimination, or anything serious between colleagues.
Any financial irregularity — off-system payment, missing cash, billing dispute.
Anything you are not sure about. If your gut is uncertain, escalate.
Escalate by end-of-day if
A complaint was resolved on the floor but should be on her radar.
A team conflict that you handled but that may need follow-up.
A doctor-counsellor friction you noticed in passing.
Anything that affects how the next day will run.
How you brief her
Crisply. Facts first, then your judgement, then what you have already done.
“Jaspreet ma'am, Mrs Sharma in cabin 2 had a mild reaction at the end of her session — redness extending beyond the treatment area. Doctor saw her within five minutes, treated, observed for 20 minutes, she has gone home with topical and a follow-up booked tomorrow. I have logged it and asked the therapist for a written note. I think we should call Mrs Sharma in the evening ourselves — do you want to make that call, or shall I?”
INNER STANCE  The FDM who escalates well is invaluable. The FDM who escalates everything is exhausting. The FDM who escalates nothing is dangerous. Find the line: anything clinical or financial or unsafe — escalate the same hour. Anything operational — handle and brief. Anything you are unsure about — default to escalating.
10.  End of Day Debrief  —  Closing the Floor
The last patient has left. The team is winding down. Take ten minutes — not thirty — to close the day properly.
With the team  —  five minutes
Gather everyone briefly. One round of ‘how did your day go?’ — each person, one sentence. You are reading energy, not collecting reports.
Acknowledge specifically. ‘Suman, you handled Mrs Sharma beautifully today. Thank you.’ ‘Jaspreet, the cabin resets were tight today even when we were behind — thank you.’
Note tomorrow's first thing. ‘Mrs Khanna is in at 10 — her birthday, please make it warm.’
Close warmly. ‘Good day, team. Sleep well. See you tomorrow.’
THIRD AFFIRMATION  ·  THE END-OF-DAY CLOSE
“Thank you, team. Today was good because each of you held your part. Sleep well. See you tomorrow.”
Solo  —  five minutes
Walk the clinic one last time. The condition you leave it in is the condition the morning team inherits.
Write the debrief note. Three bullets: what went well, what did not, what tomorrow needs to know. Send it to the BM by 8 pm.
Check that any patient callback owed today has been made or is logged for first thing tomorrow.
Switch the floor over to the closing team or close yourself, depending on the shift.
THE PSYCHOLOGY  The end-of-day acknowledgement is the highest-leverage retention tool a manager has — and the cheapest. The team member who hears her name in your closing two times a week works ten percent harder for you for the next year. The team member whose contributions are never specifically named looks for warmth elsewhere within a season.
11.  Communication Rules  —  The FDM Code
Always
Walk slowly even on a busy floor. Your pace is the floor's pace.
Greet every team member by name in the morning.
Acknowledge every waiting patient who has been there more than ten minutes.
Correct privately. Praise publicly.
Document complaints same day. No exceptions.
Follow up personally with any complaint patient within 48 hours.
Escalate anything clinical, financial, or unsafe the same hour.
Close the day with the team — every day.
Never
Never raise your voice on the floor. The floor's calm is your calm.
Never correct a team member in front of another team member or a patient.
Never let a complaint be witnessed in the open waiting area.
Never promise a refund without checking with the BM.
Never bypass a clinical opinion — the doctor decides clinical, you decide operational.
Never let a patient leave unhappy without one warm question at the door.
Never go home with a complaint undocumented.
12.  The Goal of the FDM  —  In Order of Importance
1.  Standard
The branch operates at the same standard at 6 pm as it did at 9 am. The team's energy holds, the cabins reset on time, the washroom is checked, the patients are acknowledged — not because rules are followed, but because the manager held the floor.
2.  Catch
Problems that would have escalated were caught small — the unhappy patient at the door, the team member having a hard day, the doctor's morning slipping. Caught early, all of them stay small.
3.  Flow
The day runs. Patients in, consultations done, handovers smooth, cabins reset, payments clean, follow-ups logged. The patient feels none of the operational complexity — it is invisible because you handled it.
4.  Team
The team leaves the day feeling held, named, and seen. Retention is built in small daily moments — your morning huddle, your end-of-day close, the correction conversation that was warm, the bad day that was noticed.
5.  Trust upward
The BM trusts you because you escalate well, document well, and never surprise her with something she should have heard earlier. The trust upward is what creates the autonomy that lets you run the floor.
13.  Quick Reference Card
Print this page. Keep it inside your desk drawer. Glance at it before the morning huddle.
THE THREE AFFIRMATIONS  ·  TIMING
“The Morning Close:  “Have a good day, team. Let's take care of each other and the patients.”    ·    The Patient in Wait:  “Thank you for your patience — it really matters to us.”    ·    End-of-Day:  “Thank you, team. Today was good because each of you held your part. See you tomorrow.””

THE INNER STANCE  ·  RE-READ EVERY MORNING
“You are not the supervisor. You are the conductor. Your pace is the floor's pace. Your calm is the floor's calm. Correct privately, praise publicly, catch what would fall, close the day with the team. Hold the standard the patient never sees you holding.”

THE NEVER LIST  Never raise your voice on the floor. Never correct in public. Never let a complaint be witnessed in the open. Never promise a refund without the BM. Never bypass a clinical opinion. Never let a patient leave unhappy without one warm question. Never go home with a complaint undocumented.
